transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. Attorneys for Krista Pike, the woman
who received two lethal injections in Tennessee yesterday and still lived, were told she is
in critical condition. One of her attorneys, Stephen Farrell, called for the governor to
commute her death sentence after what he called "cruel and unusual punishment."
We presented evidence that due to her blood condition, venous access would be difficult,
and that this type of prolonged execution that she didn't want to happen would happen.
Her attorneys said she had a blood condition that makes it difficult to administer injections.
Pike was sentenced to death for a murder she committed at age 18. She would have been the
first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Tennessee Republican Governor
Bill Lee has put executions in the state on hold and called for a third-party review to
determine what caused the failed execution. A prosecutor in New York now says he didn't
have access to full transcripts of a woman's account of being raped at Cornell University
in 2024 when he decided not to pursue the case. District Attorney Matthew Van Houten
says he stopped the investigation after only reviewing the woman's signed statement. NPR's
Brian Mann reports.
Van Houten has said the former student, who alleged in a recent civil lawsuit that she
was gang-raped by seven male students, gave a different account to campus police two years
ago, describing her participation in drug use and sex at a frat party as "voluntary,
conscious and consensual." But now more full transcripts of the woman's interviews with
campus police investigators have been reported by multiple news outlets. They show she described
the incident at the time in graphic terms as rape. In a statement to WSKG Radio, Van
Houten says he didn't see that information before stopping the investigation. "If it's
actual, we absolutely should have been informed about what Jane Doe said to police Van Houten
said." Brian Mann, NPR News, Ithaca, New York.
Starting today, states will be paying for a larger share of the bill to run the SNAP
Food Assistance Program. NPR's Julianna Kim reports federal funding for costs, including
state SNAP workers, will shrink by half.
Last year's massive Republican tax and spending law, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act,
noted major changes to how SNAP is funded, shifting more of the costs onto states rather
than the federal government. As a result, states may need to spend two to three times
more in the future in order to keep the Food Assistance Program running. That's according
to the Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality. The key question now is how states will afford
these new costs to SNAP. Policy experts say states may need to raise taxes, cut funding
for other programs, or reduce access to food benefits. And it comes as SNAP participation
is already rapidly dropping. Julianna Kim, NPR News.
Major U.S. stock indexes rose slightly today. The S&P 500 rose nearly two-tenths of a percent,
breaking a three-day losing streak. This is NPR News.
Political power in state legislatures and governors' offices is at stake in more than
one-third of the states this year. Voters in 46 states will choose over 6,100 lawmakers
in November, and 36 states will hold gubernatorial elections. The races could be important in
determining the fate of President Trump's agenda, as state officials either aid or resist
policies about immigration, social safety net programs, and voting procedures.
Two new contenders have joined the ranks for the world's loudest bird, the bear-throated
bell bird, and the red-legged siriama. And PR's Ari Daniel has more.
Researchers have long studied the pitch and rhythm of bird vocalizations, but technology
now allows the measurement of volume. While a Ph.D. student at UMass Amherst, João Menezes
and his advisor managed to record the volume of 123 bird species across western Massachusetts
and Brazil, many for the first time. Even in your backyard, you feel like an early naturalist.
The range was staggering, an 800-fold difference between the softest species, a kind of hummingbird,
all the way up to a very loud trio of species. Comparable to the level of a jackhammer. Larger
species and those with wider mouth openings tend to sing louder, but it's still not clear
what's driving all the variety. Ari Daniel, NPR News.
French Soccer star Zinedine Zidane famously headbutted Italy's Marco Mazzarazzi during
the 2006 World Cup final, ending his career with a red card. 20 years later, Zidane will
face Italy again tomorrow, but this time as France's head coach. This is NPR.

topics.text: Krista Pike receives two lethal injections in Tennessee and survives; attorneys call for sentence commutation
New York prosecutor says he lacked full transcripts when declining to pursue Cornell University rape case
States begin paying larger share of SNAP food assistance program costs under Republican tax law
S&P 500 stock index rises nearly two-tenths of a percent, breaking three-day losing streak
Voters in 46 states will choose over 6,100 lawmakers in November; 36 states hold gubernatorial elections
Researchers identify two new contenders for world's loudest bird species using new measurement technology
Zinedine Zidane faces Italy as France head coach, 20 years after infamous World Cup headbutt
